rv.q: This challenging, shattering and strikingly humane play from celebrated writer-director Robert Icke pushes back against such a simplistic assessment, instead using Moat’s grim story to frame potent questions about toxic masculinity.
Yet it is coruscating. It transmits indelible images. Not moving but transfixing.
It amply justifies main-stage attention, and deserves to tour, too.
Icke is one of the most gifted theatre artists working today – his magnificent 2024. Oedipus has just won a string of awards – but for all its intensity, Manhunt feels like it’s hedging its bets.
The play’s moral neutrality is spineless.
Just when you think the play is going to eclipse the much more conventional Punch, the piece begins to lose focus.
But somehow, it lacks Icke’s usual ability to winnow complex source material into one coherent message.
But this play never quite delivers in its dramatic power or its psychological insights.
Robert Icke, directing his own text, generates theatrical excitement, and, in Edward-Cook’s Moat, a performance that could be a contender for next year’s award ceremonies.
Icke’s take on the subject is an intense and powerful experience.
Icke’s direction and command of an excellent cast playing many roles is disciplined and often audacious.
While definitely not a hagiography, Manhunt still suffers from a lack of nuance, but Edward- Cook’s towering, chilling performance makes up for some of the flaws.
Icke’s Royal Court debut is certainly thought-provoking.
The Royal Court, known as the writers’ theatre, once again delivers an intense, conflicting story designed to unsettle the spectator.

cn.t: Icke's visceral, risk-taking exploration of the Raoul Moat case divides critics. Most praise Samuel Edward-Cook's terrifying performance and the production's intense, transfixing staging, though some question whether it achieves the compassion it seeks.
